title: Solid-state batteries: why they are so hard to build
hook: Twice the range, always five years away. The battery already exists in buses. Four hard problems keep it out of your car.

lines.text: Twice the range, charging in ten minutes, no fire risk. That is the promise of the solid-state battery.
Car makers have been announcing it for about ten years. And it is still always a few years away.
Here is the surprise: solid-state batteries already exist. They have been driving around in buses for years.
So the real question is not whether they work. It is why they are so hard to build for cars.
To see why, we first need to look inside a normal battery.

lines.text: A lithium-ion battery has two sides that can store lithium. Think of them as two shelves.
When you charge, lithium moves to one shelf, the anode. When you drive, it moves back to the other one, the cathode.
The lithium travels as charged particles, called ions, through a liquid in between. That liquid is the electrolyte.
Electrons cannot pass through that liquid. They have to take the detour through the wire, and that detour is your electric current.
A thin plastic sheet, the separator, keeps the two shelves from touching each other.

lines.text: The liquid electrolyte does its job well. Ions move through it easily, and it seeps into every pore of the shelves.
But it is a flammable solvent. If a cell is damaged or overheats, this liquid is what burns.
And it rules out the best anode material there is. You will see why in a moment.
The idea of the solid-state battery is simple: replace the liquid with a solid material that still lets lithium ions pass.

lines.text: Most people think the main gain is safety. The bigger prize is hidden in the anode.
Today’s anode is graphite. It works like a shelf: for every lithium atom it stores, it needs six carbon atoms to hold it.
The ideal anode would be pure lithium metal. No shelf, only cargo. Per gram, it stores about ten times as much.
For the whole cell, developers aim for roughly one and a half times the energy at the same weight.
In 2025, a Mercedes test car with lithium-metal cells drove 1,205 kilometres on one charge. Its pack held 25 percent more energy at the same size.

quiz.q: Why could a solid electrolyte give an electric car more range?

options.text: The solid electrolyte itself stores extra lithium
options.why: The electrolyte is only the road for the ions. It stores no usable energy, whether it is liquid or solid.

options.text: It may allow a lithium-metal anode, which stores far more per gram than graphite
options.why: The solid itself stores nothing. Its value is that it might make the lithium-metal anode usable, and that anode needs no heavy shelf.

options.text: Solid materials are lighter than the liquid they replace
options.why: Usually the opposite is true. Ceramic electrolytes are denser than the liquid. The weight is saved at the anode, not at the electrolyte.

quiz.explain: Think of a delivery van. Today’s anode is a van full of shelving: for every parcel of lithium, it carries six parcels’ worth of rack made of carbon. A lithium-metal anode is a van with no shelves at all, packed with parcels only. The same van carries far more. But parcels without shelves slide around, and in a battery that sliding shows up as needles that cause short circuits. The solid electrolyte is meant to be the wall that keeps the load in place. So the solid part is the enabler, and the extra range comes from the anode behind it.

lines.text: So why not use lithium metal with the liquid we already have? Because of the way lithium grows back when you charge.
It does not settle as a smooth layer. It grows in tiny needles, called dendrites.
Charge after charge, a needle grows through the liquid and through the thin separator, until it touches the other side.
That is a short circuit inside the cell. The energy is released at once, as heat, in a flammable liquid.
So the hope was simple: a hard, solid electrolyte would be a wall that needles cannot pierce.

lines.text: And here comes the first surprise. The needles grow through hard ceramic too.
Lithium is soft enough to cut with a knife. But it finds tiny cracks, and the borders between the grains of the ceramic.
Inside a crack, it acts like a wedge. The crack widens, the lithium follows, and in the end the cell is shorted again.
This happens mostly at high current, which means during fast charging. So the limit shows up exactly where the promise was biggest.
Researchers still argue about the exact mechanism. Finer grains and special coatings help, but the problem is not closed.

lines.text: The second problem sounds trivial, and it is not. A liquid touches every surface. Two solids touch only at their high points.
Lay two sheets of sandpaper on top of each other. They meet at a few tips. Ions can cross only at those tips.
It gets worse while the battery works. The anode grows thicker when charging and thinner when discharging. The cell breathes.
With every breath, contact points break. In the lab, the fix is brute force: steel plates press the cell together.
Lab cells often needed 20 megapascals or more. That is the pressure two kilometres deep in the sea. A car can supply perhaps a tenth of that.

quiz.q: A new solid-state cell works perfectly in the lab, clamped between thick steel plates. Why is that not yet good news for a car?

options.text: Steel plates conduct electricity and improve the result artificially
options.why: The plates are not part of the circuit. They help mechanically, by pressing the layers together.

options.text: The clamp hides the contact problem, and a car cannot carry that pressure
options.why: High pressure keeps the solids touching while the cell breathes. In a car, the plates needed for it would eat up the weight advantage.

options.text: Lab cells use purer lithium than a factory could ever get
options.why: Purity is not the issue here. The same cell would fail in the lab too, as soon as the pressure is removed.

quiz.explain: Imagine two bricks with a sheet of paper between them. Press hard, and the paper touches both bricks everywhere. Let go and shake them a little, and the paper touches only here and there. A solid-state cell behaves like that. Ions can cross only where the layers really touch, and the anode keeps moving, because it swells and shrinks with every charge. Steel plates in the lab press everything together with a force no car could carry. So the honest test of a cell is how it behaves at low pressure. You will see in a moment why one result from this month got so much attention.

</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="326" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="353" class="mid ts">the bus: truly solid, but heated all the time</text>
</g>

lines.text: Third problem: there is no perfect solid electrolyte. There are three families, and each one has a catch.
Sulfides conduct ions as well as a liquid. But with moisture they release hydrogen sulfide, a toxic gas. Factories need extremely dry rooms.
Oxide ceramics are stable and safe to handle. But they are brittle like a dinner plate, and have to be baked at around a thousand degrees.
Polymers, which means plastics, are easy to produce. But they conduct well only when warm, at 60 to 80 degrees.
That is the bus from the beginning. Its polymer battery is truly solid, and it has to be kept hot all the time.

scenes.svg:
<g data-l="0" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="40" class="mid ts fm">the factory: kilometres of one thin layer</text>
<circle cx="64" cy="104" r="30" class="fp si"/><circle cx="64" cy="104" r="8" class="fn si s1"/>
<circle cx="336" cy="104" r="30" class="fp si"/><circle cx="336" cy="104" r="8" class="fn si s1"/>

</g>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<circle cx="110" cy="214" r="28" class="fn sm"/><text x="110" y="262" class="mid ts fm">a human hair</text>
<rect x="220" y="208" width="120" height="10" rx="2" class="fd"/><text x="280" y="262" class="mid ts fd tb">the layer: thinner</text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="pop"><circle cx="214" cy="74" r="9" class="fn sc pulse"/></g>
<text x="200" y="160" class="mid ts fc tb" data-l="2" data-fx="up">one pinhole = one failed cell</text>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<path d="M50 296 C110 340 240 356 350 360" class="fn sb s3"/>

<text x="200" y="388" class="mid ts fm">over 30 years of getting cheaper</text>

lines.text: Even with the right material, the hardest part may be the factory.
The solid layer has to be thinner than a human hair, and free of holes over many square metres.
One pinhole is enough for a needle to get through. And one bad cell among thousands can spoil a whole battery pack.
Factories for liquid batteries have had more than thirty years to become this cheap. A new technology has to compete with that from day one.

scenes.title: And is it really safer?
scenes.svg:
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">

</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="210" y="40" width="166" height="120" rx="14" class="fp"/>

</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="196" class="mid ts fm">heat when the cell fails</text>
<rect x="120" y="216" width="46" height="90" rx="6" class="fm"/><text x="143" y="326" class="mid ts">normal cell</text>
<rect x="234" y="222" width="46" height="84" rx="6" class="fc"/><text x="257" y="326" class="mid ts">solid, cracked</text>

</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="344" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>

lines.text: What about the safety promise? It is true only in part.
Without the flammable liquid, an ordinary fire becomes less likely. That part holds.
But lithium metal itself is highly reactive. In 2022, researchers at Sandia National Laboratories calculated what happens when such cells fail.
Their result: if the solid layer cracks, such a cell can heat up about as much as a normal one. With lithium metal inside, there is always something that can react.
So: safer in many cases, yes. Automatically safe, no.

lines.text: So where are we, at the end of 2026?
Samsung names the second half of 2027 for its first mass production. Toyota speaks of 2027 to 2028. Both mean small numbers, for expensive models.
And this month, the company QuantumScape reported a fully solid cell that survived 1,000 charge cycles without a press, at normal air pressure.
That goes straight at problem two. But it was a small test cell, and by then it had lost about a fifth of its capacity.
Most analysts expect solid-state cells in ordinary cars after 2030, not before.

lines.text: One more thing makes this race hard. The target is moving.
Ordinary lithium-ion batteries get better and cheaper every year. Some manufacturers have announced charging for hundreds of kilometres in about five minutes.
And in between sits a mixed form: semi-solid cells, a gel with a little liquid. They are already on the road in some Chinese cars.
So when you read “solid-state” in a headline, check which of the two is meant.

quiz.q: A startup reports record energy density. The test: a coin-sized cell at 60 °C, 100 cycles. What is the most reasonable reading?

options.text: Cars with this battery will arrive within a year or two
options.why: From a coin cell to a car cell usually takes many years. Scaling up is where most candidates fail.

options.text: It must be fake, because solid-state batteries do not work
options.why: The result can be perfectly real. Small, warm cells do work well. The open question is full size, room temperature and low pressure.

options.text: A promising material result, but still far from a car battery
options.why: Coin size, warm temperature and few cycles avoid three of the four hard problems. The result says something about the material, not about a product.

quiz.explain: A coin cell is to a car battery what a paper plane is to an airliner. Both fly, and the paper plane proves a real principle. But it does not tell you whether the big machine can be built, what it costs, or how long it lasts. In a tiny cell, there are few places for a crack or a pinhole. Warmth makes ions move more easily and softens the contact problem. And a hundred cycles is about a tenth of what a car needs. So the right reaction is neither excitement nor dismissal. It is to ask about size, temperature and pressure, cycles, and whether the cell is fully solid.

scenes.title: How to read the next headline
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="38" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">four questions for any battery headline</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="62" width="352" height="48" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="54" cy="86" r="14" class="fk sa"/><text x="54" y="91" class="mid ts fa tb">1</text><text x="82" y="91" class="tm">Cell size: coin or car?</text></g><g data-l="2" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="124" width="352" height="48" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="54" cy="148" r="14" class="fk sa"/><text x="54" y="153" class="mid ts fa tb">2</text><text x="82" y="153" class="tm">Temperature and pressure?</text></g><g data-l="3" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="186" width="352" height="48" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="54" cy="210" r="14" class="fk sa"/><text x="54" y="215" class="mid ts fa tb">3</text><text x="82" y="215" class="tm">Cycles and charging speed?</text></g><g data-l="4" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="248" width="352" height="48" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="54" cy="272" r="14" class="fk sa"/><text x="54" y="277" class="mid ts fa tb">4</text><text x="82" y="277" class="tm">Fully solid or semi-solid?</text></g>
<text x="200" y="346" class="mid tm fb tb" data-l="4" data-fx="up" data-d="4">no answers = advertising</text>

lines.text: You can now judge the next battery announcement yourself. Ask four questions.
How big was the cell: the size of a coin, or the size of a real car cell?
At what temperature, and under what pressure, did it run?
How many cycles did it survive, and how fast was it charged?
And is it fully solid, or semi-solid? If an announcement answers none of these, it is advertising.

scenes.title: The short version
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="38" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">not one missing invention: four problems</text>

<text x="200" y="212" class="mid ts fm" data-l="1" data-fx="up" data-d="4.5">all four: being solved step by step</text>
<text x="200" y="262" class="mid tm fa tb" data-l="2" data-fx="up">the prize is real: lithium metal</text>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">

<text x="200" y="327" class="mid tm">first in expensive cars, late this decade</text>
</g>

lines.text: The short version: the solid-state battery is not one single invention that is still missing.
It is four hard problems at once: needles, contact, materials and the factory. Each one is being solved step by step.
The prize is real, because lithium metal stores so much more. That is why billions keep flowing into it.
Expect it first in expensive cars, late in this decade. And until then, enjoy how good the ordinary battery has become.

takeaways: A solid-state battery replaces the flammable liquid electrolyte with a solid that still lets lithium ions pass.
The main prize is not safety but the anode: lithium metal stores about ten times as much per gram as graphite.
Problem one: lithium needles (dendrites) grow through cracks and grain borders even in hard ceramic, mostly during fast charging.
Problem two: solids touch only at their tips, and the cell breathes. Lab cells needed pressures that no car can carry.
Problems three and four: every solid electrolyte has a catch (toxic gas, brittleness or heat), and the layer must be made thin and free of holes at factory scale.
Check any headline with four questions: cell size, temperature and pressure, cycles and charging speed, fully solid or semi-solid.
